source: That branch of the lake of Como which extends southwards between two unbroken chains of mountains, and is all bays and gulfs as the mountains advance and recede, narrows down at one point into the form of a river, between a promontory on one side and a wide shore on the other; and the bridge which here links the two banks seems to emphasize this transformation, and to mark the point at which the lake ends and the Adda begins, only to become a lake once more where the banks draw farther apart again, letting the water broaden out and expand into new gulfs and bays. The country bordering the lake, formed by the deposits of three great torrents, is backed by two neighbouring mountains, one called San Martino, and the other, in the Lombard dialect, the Resegone, from its saw-like row of peaks; so that on first seeing it — so long as it is in profile — looking northwards, for instance, from the ramparts of Milan — one can pick it out at once, on the name alone, from the vast and lengthy range of other mountains of obscurer name and more ordinary form. For a considerable stretch the country rises slowly and continuously; then it breaks up into little hills and valleys and into steep and level tracts, following the structure of the two mountains and the erosion of the water. The shore itself, intersected by the beds of torrents, is almost entirely gravel and pebbles; the rest is fields and vineyards, and scattered towns, villages and farms, with here and there a wood extending right on up the mountain-side. Lecco, which is the largest of these towns and gives its name to the district, lies on the lakeside not far from the bridge, and is even apt to find itself partly in the lake when this is high; it is a big town nowadays, well on the way to becoming a city. At the time of the events which we are about to describe, this township which was already of some importance, was also fortified, and so had the honour of housing a commandant and the advantage of a permanent garrison of Spanish soldiers, who taught modesty to the wives and daughters of the town, tickled up the shoulders of an occasional husband and father, and, towards the end of summer, never failed to scatter themselves among the vineyards, to thin out the grapes and lighten the labours of the vintage for the peasants. Paths and tracks used to run — and still do — from one to another of these villages, from the mountain heights to the lakeside, and from one precipice to the other. Sometimes they run steep, sometimes level, and often drop suddenly and bury themselves between two walls, from which, when one looks up, only a patch of sky and some mountain peak can be discerned. Sometimes they come out on open terraces; thence the eye ranges over prospects of varying extent, always full of interest and always changing, as each point of vantage takes in different aspects of the vast landscape, and as one part or the other is foreshortened, or stands out, or disappears. One can see a piece here, another there, and then again a long stretch of that great varied mirror of the water; on this side the lake is shut in at one end, or rather lost among the ins and outs and groupings of the mountains, then spreads out again between more mountains, unfolding one by one, and reflected upside down in the water with the villages on the shores; on the other side is more river, then lake, then river again, losing itself in a shining coil among the mountains, which follow it, getting smaller and smaller until they too are almost lost in the horizon. The very spot from which so many different views can be seen itself appears in views from every side. The mountain on whose foothills you are walking unfolds its cliffs and pinnacles above and around you, each standing out on its own and changing at every step, turning what had just seemed a single ridge into a whole series of ridges, and showing on a height something that a moment before had seemed down on the shore; the quiet and cosy character of these foothills pleasantly tempers the wildness around, and is a foil for the grandeur of the rest of the landscape.

The estate of Veradine Holloway, which came to this court in the ordinary way of contested probate, presents a difficulty that is not evidentiary but conceptual, for the documents are authentic and the witnesses agree, and the parties themselves have conceded the chronology; yet the three claimants ask this bench to decide what a word meant in the mouth of a woman who said it twice, in two instruments eleven years apart, and in the interval had sold a mill, buried a brother, and come to call certain people her family who were not her family when the first instrument was signed, so that the court must determine whether the later usage governs the earlier, or whether the earlier survives as a fixed definition and the later merely repeats it.

The first claimant, Dorrit Holloway, who is the decedent's nephew by her elder brother, who managed the mill for nine years without salary, who asks the court to read the phrase "my household" as it stood in 1988, relies upon an argument of simple priority: because the first will defined the household by enumeration, because that enumeration named him, because no later instrument revoked the definition in terms.

The argument has a surface strength that the court does not dismiss; it would be decisive if a definition, once written, held its meaning against the life that continued around it.

But a will is not a statute, and the testator who drafts it is also the person who lives afterward among the words she chose, altering, without clerical formality, the persons to whom those words refer.

The second claimant, Ilse Morrow, who was not born into the family but entered it through the decedent's late companion, is content to concede the enumeration of 1988, provided the court acknowledges what the record shows plainly; and she offers four letters in which the decedent speaks of her as a daughter.

Counsel for the first claimant, who moved to exclude those letters as extrinsic to the instrument, whose objection the court overruled at the hearing, has renewed the point in writing, and it deserves an answer, for the rule excluding extrinsic evidence protects the integrity of a written disposition, but it does not require a court to pretend that a phrase whose referents are persons can be construed without knowing who the persons were at the moment of writing.

The letters are therefore admitted, not to contradict the second instrument, but to identify the persons it contemplates.

So read, the 1999 will appears to do something the first claimant denies: it repeats the phrase; it does not repeat the list, and the omission is not accidental, for the drafter struck the enumeration in a marked hand and initialed the margin.

Here the third claimant, Peter Vance, enters the dispute on a narrower ground: he does not quarrel with either construction, but asks the court to find that his mother's lifetime gift of the mill proceeds was an advancement against her share, so that whatever the household means, the accounting must be adjusted, and his siblings' portions reduced accordingly, and his own restored.

The court finds for the second claimant on the central question and for the third in part: the phrase "my household," as used in the operative instrument of 1999, denotes those persons who stood in the decedent's affection and daily care at the date of that instrument, and Ilse Morrow is among them. This does not disinherit the first claimant, whose interest in the residuary estate is untouched, whose service to the mill the court records with respect, though the law affords no remedy for unpaid labor undertaken as kindness and asserted only after a death, and though the equities are not nothing.

The advancement claim, which rests on a contemporaneous ledger entry in the decedent's hand, succeeds.

The estate will be distributed accordingly, which is to say on the construction the court has given, and because the parties have borne the cost of a dispute that was never dishonest, and because no claim here was advanced in the bad faith that would justify a different order, each side will bear its own costs, which is the only disposition the record supports; let the decree be entered.

The estate of Horace Venable, which came into this court not as a quarrel over money but as a quarrel over what a life had meant to the people who stood nearest it, must be resolved on the documents and on the conduct that surrounded them, for the will of 1996 is clear on its face and the codicil of 2011 is clear on its own, and the difficulty lies entirely in the space between them; so I begin with the earlier instrument, which divided the farm in equal thirds among the three children, and I propose to read it as the testator's settled mind, a mind that did not change merely because the body weakened, for a man may grow frail and still know what he wants, and so, before any party asks me to set the codicil aside on the ground that illness clouded judgment, the court must first ask whether illness in fact clouded anything at all, and whether the later words, read in their own light, so plainly contradict the earlier that both cannot stand together.

The petitioner, Margaret Venable, who farmed the land for nineteen years without wages, who buried her mother in the spring of 2008, and who has produced ledgers in her own hand, asks the court to enforce the codicil in her favor; her argument has three limbs: because she alone remained when the others left for the city, because the codicil names her expressly as the one who stayed, and because the testator signed it before two witnesses whose competence no party disputes.

Against this, her brother Daniel advances a single proposition, and it is a formidable one: that the codicil, whatever its words, was procured in a house where only one voice was ever heard.

He points to the testator's isolation in the final years, which he characterizes as cultivated rather than accidental; his claim is simple enough: that proximity became leverage in a household where no third party ever entered.

I accept a portion of this, for the evidence does establish that Margaret controlled the correspondence and screened the telephone, but I decline to treat control as coercion where the record shows the testator still transacting business, still refusing advice, still writing letters of his own; the inference Daniel presses would require me to equate opportunity with its exercise.

The youngest, Clara, who has asked for nothing but to be heard, who was absent from the farm for twenty-two years and does not pretend otherwise, takes a different path altogether, and her submission deserves careful notice, since it raises the only question that genuinely troubles me, which is not whether the codicil was signed freely, nor whether Margaret earned what she claims, but whether the testator understood that his later words would operate to extinguish what his earlier words had promised, when the two documents were never placed side by side before him and no lawyer read them together in his presence.

On this I find the evidence thin; the drafting solicitor cannot recall the meeting, and his file note runs to four lines.

Thinness, however, cuts both ways: a gap in the record is not proof of a defect; the burden rests on the party alleging the defect, and Clara has not discharged it; nor does the court supply by suspicion what the objector has failed to supply by evidence, though the temptation is real.

I therefore hold the codicil valid in its operation: it reduces the shares of Daniel and Clara, and it does so because the testator, who had watched one child feed his cattle through four winters while the others telephoned at Christmas, chose to reward what he could see, and chose it in words that admit of no second reading.

That conclusion does not, however, exhaust the matter, which has a residue the parties have not addressed.

Equity retains a modest office here, which I exercise sparingly: because the codicil speaks of the farm and is silent as to the proceeds of the timber sold in 2010, and because that silence cannot be filled by a document that never contemplated the transaction, those proceeds fall to be distributed under the earlier instrument, which the codicil nowhere revokes in whole; the division is accordingly as follows.

The estate of the late cartographer Helmut Oyeleye, which comprised a narrow house on Quarry Terrace, a small annuity, and some four hundred engraved plates of coastline, descends in this court by a path that is neither simple nor, as the parties would have it, obvious, because the will executed in the ninth year before his death was superseded in part and revoked in part by a later instrument; and it falls to me to determine, upon the pleadings before me, whether the second instrument, which was drawn by a solicitor long since struck off and witnessed by two neighbours who have since recanted, can be permitted to stand against the first, so that the plates, which the testator's daughter claims by express devise and the nephew claims by residue, may pass entire to one hand rather than be severed.

The daughter, Imogen Oyeleye, who kept the house for eleven years, who paid the rates out of her own wages, and who alone among the claimants proposes to maintain the collection undispersed, advances three propositions: first, that her father was of settled mind when he signed; second, that the plates were promised to her orally and repeatedly; third, that the nephew's interest arises only by default.

I take these in order, for they are not of equal weight: the first is a question of fact, the second a question of evidence, the third a question of construction, and nothing is gained by trying all three at once.

As to capacity, the medical notes tendered by the nephew, which record a diagnosis of vascular decline in the spring of that year, do not carry the burden he places upon them; a diagnosis is not an incapacity, and the attending physician, who was called and cross-examined, conceded the point without reluctance.

The testator continued to correct proofs, to dictate letters that survive in his own numbered sequence, and to conduct a correspondence with a Rotterdam printer; he was able to explain, when the solicitor's clerk asked him, why the house should go one way and the plates another; the account he gave then, which the clerk recorded in a hand nobody has sought to impugn, is enough to dispose of the objection.

As to the oral promise, I find the daughter's evidence credible but legally inert, for a promise to leave property, which the law requires to be embodied in due form before it can bind an estate, which may be sincerely given and sincerely received, is not a disposition; the testimony of her neighbour was honest and the testimony of her employer was careful, but neither witness could do more than establish that the testator said what he meant, when what is in issue is whether he wrote it and whether the writing survived his second thoughts.

The nephew, Carrick Abernethy, asks me to read the residuary clause expansively; his counsel argues the plates were never specifically described in the later instrument.

Here I must disagree, and say why plainly: the clause devises "my engraved work and the instruments thereof"; the phrase is not elegant, yet it is not ambiguous; it attaches to the plates and to nothing else, since no other engraved work existed.

The nephew's secondary argument is weaker still; he contends that the daughter forfeited her interest by selling two plates in the year before her father died, but that transaction was authorised in writing, the proceeds were applied to the testator's care, the sum was accounted for to the penny, and the testator himself acknowledged the sale in a letter.

I therefore hold as follows: the later instrument is admitted to probate; the specific devise of the engraved work takes effect in favour of the daughter, who shall hold the four hundred plates subject to the charge hereafter described and shall not dispose of them except with leave of this court; the residue, including the annuity and such part of the house as remains after the mortgage is discharged, falls to the nephew, who has in my view been treated by the family with a coldness that is not for me to remedy, since the law of succession measures entitlement rather than affection, and I decline to invent a remedy where the testator declined to leave one.

Costs will follow the event, save that the medical evidence, which was reasonably obtained, shall be borne equally.

The house, which the daughter has occupied throughout, shall not be sold before the expiry of twelve months, so that she may seek alternative accommodation, and so that the valuation, which both parties have contested from the beginning, may be revised by an assessor jointly appointed; the parties shall file their nominations within twenty-eight days, failing which I shall appoint one myself; this is the judgment of the court.

The estate of Hollis Verrance, which consisted of a timber mill, two parcels of upland pasture, and a cash account whose balance has not been disputed, comes before this court because the testator executed two instruments within a single autumn and left no clear statement of which was to govern, and his children, who were present at neither signing, have each built an elaborate case upon that silence; the eldest, Marion, who has held the mill's books for eleven years, now asks the court to read the later instrument as a nullity, since her father, as she contends, was by then unable to follow a recital of his own holdings, and the second document, as the attesting clerk conceded under questioning, was prepared in an afternoon by a stranger to the family, who had been fetched from the county seat that morning.

Against this the second claimant, Dell, who left the valley at nineteen and returned only after the funeral, who has produced no witness to his father's condition, who nevertheless asks the court to treat the later instrument as the plain and final voice of a man entitled to change his mind, offers an argument of a different shape: if infirmity is to be inferred from the brevity of a signing, then every deliberate testator is suspect; if a stranger's hand is disqualifying, then no notary may draft; if a daughter's long service purchases a veto, then the will is no longer the testator's.

The court does not find this second argument empty, and it answers the first at its strongest point: though Marion's evidence of her father's decline is detailed and in places affecting, it establishes forgetfulness rather than incapacity.

The medical testimony, which was drawn from a physician who had examined the testator twice in the relevant season, is careful on precisely this distinction; it describes a man who could not recall the acreage of his own pasture but could state without hesitation whom he wished to have it.

That distinction governs the whole of what follows, since the law, which asks only whether a testator knew his property in kind and his natural objects of bounty, does not require him to recite a schedule, and this court declines to invent a standard which no prudent person over seventy could hope to satisfy.

But Dell's argument, which seeks to make the later instrument self-sufficient, which treats its formal regularity as the end of the inquiry, overreaches at its own strongest point; for the question that remains is not whether the testator understood what he was doing, but whether he was left alone to do it, and here the record is less obliging to him, and here the court must weigh the fact that the stranger-drafter was engaged by Dell's own correspondence, which arrived in the valley eight days before the signing and named the terms it afterwards produced.

The court does not treat this as proof of coercion, and it declines to say that a son may not urge his case upon his father.

It is one thing to argue; it is another to arrange the room, to supply the draftsman, and to absent the only other interested party when the paper is laid down.

Still, the law of undue influence demands more than opportunity: it demands that the will be shown to be another's and not the testator's, and on this record that showing fails, for the later instrument departs from the earlier in one clause only, and that clause gives the mill to Marion outright, and it gives Dell the upland pasture he had asked for in writing.

A man who is being overborne does not usually confirm his antagonist in the most valuable asset: the later instrument, read whole, is the act of a father settling an old quarrel on terms he evidently thought fair, and the quarrel itself, which both children described at length and in substantially the same way, which neither could recount without betraying how much of it was still unfinished, explains the one change better than any theory of imposition, because the testator, to end a dispute he had no further strength for, divided what could be divided while he still had the standing to divide it.

Judgment accordingly goes for the later instrument, which the court admits to probate in its entirety.

The costs of the proceeding, which have been considerable, shall be borne by the estate rather than by either claimant, because neither position was frivolous and because the ambiguity that occasioned this litigation was the testator's own, who might have spared his children a season of it with a single sentence of explanation, and the court directs that the mill accounts be rendered to Dell within sixty days, which is the only relief his pleading now requires; the rest is for the parties to carry out of this room themselves.

The estate of Hollis Verrin, which consisted of a dry-goods warehouse, two unimproved parcels at the river bend, and a portfolio of municipal bonds, comes before this court in a posture of unusual difficulty, since the decedent executed three instruments in the last eleven years of his life and destroyed none of them, and the family has, with a persistence that deserves a better object, treated each as the only one that counts; and so the court is obliged to determine which document governs, to say at the outset that nothing in the record suggests fraud, for the witnesses who attended the second signing, and whose recollections differ only in small particulars, agree that the decedent was lucid when the pages were brought to him, able to read them aloud without prompting, though his hand trembled as he signed, so that the strokes thinned at the end, and the final letters run shallow.

The elder daughter, Adrienne, who managed the warehouse for nine years without salary, who advanced the decedent some forty thousand dollars during the credit panic, and who now asks the court to set aside the later instruments altogether, rests her claim on three pillars: because the 2014 will names her sole residuary legatee, because the subsequent documents were drafted by a nephew who stood to gain, and because the decedent's letters of that period speak warmly and repeatedly of her stewardship.

Her brother Dermot answers in kind: the warehouse books, he says, show salary drawn in the form of inventory, and the panic loans were repaid in 2016, though the repayment was recorded as a gift for tax purposes.

The younger sister, Lenore, who took no part in the business and asked nothing of it during the decedent's life, advances a narrower argument, which has the merit of resting on paper rather than on memory: she points to the 2021 codicil.

That codicil, which was executed in a hospital room and witnessed by two nurses who had no interest in the estate, purports to divide the residue in equal thirds, subject as it is to the conditions stated in its second clause, and it bears a notation in the decedent's hand that the court finds difficult to read as anything but deliberate.

Dermot's objection, which asks the court to disregard the codicil for want of capacity, and which rests principally on the attending physician's note of that morning, has some force, but it founders on the evidence actually before me, which includes the nurses' contemporaneous entries, and which shows a patient who answered questions about the date and the weather correctly, and who conversed about the warehouse roof, requiring the court to conclude that the burden has not been carried, since a single notation of drowsiness is not incapacity, and the law has never required perfect clarity.

I turn, therefore, to construe the codicil's second clause, and the construction is less obscure than counsel have made it appear.

The clause purports to condition each share on continued ownership of the warehouse; no sale is contemplated; the warehouse was sold in 2022 by agreement of all three, and the proceeds were deposited jointly, and the condition is thereby satisfied in substance, if not in the letter the drafter chose.

Equity does not forfeit a legacy on a technicality of this order: the condition was directed at preserving the business for the family, and where the family itself has unanimously converted the asset, the purpose survives the form, the proceeds stand in the warehouse's place, and no beneficiary has been prejudiced.

Three conclusions follow. The 2021 codicil governs; the earlier instruments are superseded to the extent of inconsistency; the residue is to be divided in equal thirds among the three children, who shall take the bond portfolio and the river parcels in kind, and who may partition by agreement within ninety days. As to Adrienne's advances, the equities are different: the loans, which the books record as repaid, which the tax filings describe as forgiven, cannot now be revived by testimony alone, when the claimant herself signed the filings, choosing to characterize the transfer as she did, while the decedent was alive to contradict her.

The claim for reimbursement of her unsalaried years, which rests on no writing at all, is dismissed.

This court is not indifferent to the hardship of that result, which falls on the one child who worked, but the law of wills must prefer the instrument to the merit, and the decedent had every opportunity to reward her expressly, if he had wished the record to say what his sister now says it meant; and so the estate is distributed as above, with costs to be borne by the estate rather than by any party, since no claim here was frivolous. Judgment accordingly.

The estate of Dorotea Venn, which consisted of a timber house above the orchard terraces, three accounts at the mutual bank, and a half-share in a quarry no longer worked, falls to be divided according to a will drawn nine years before her death, and the court must therefore decide whether that instrument, which her eldest son disputes on grounds of capacity, continues to govern, or whether the later holograph produced by the younger daughter has power to displace it — a question that cannot be answered by comparing signatures alone, since the parties have asked the court to weigh not merely the hand but the circumstances in which the hand moved, so that, before accepting either page as the last word of a woman now beyond examination, the reasoning must begin where the dispute itself began, with the autumn she stopped keeping her own ledgers.

The eldest son, who farmed the terraces for eleven years without wages, who repaired the roof twice at his own cost, and who now asks the court to treat that labour as a contribution in kind, bases his claim on the ledgers themselves: the entries thin after the autumn in question, the handwriting slopes, the sums refuse to balance by amounts too small to be fraud and too regular to be accident.

From this he argues that his mother's competence had already begun to fail when she signed the first will; the inference is tempting, but it mistakes fatigue for incapacity, since a woman of eighty may keep poor books and still know exactly whom she intends to favour.

The younger daughter, who nursed her mother through the last two winters, advances the opposite reading of the same evidence; her argument is the stronger in logic, though not in the end decisive: the very decline that her brother invokes to void the earlier document would equally have clouded the later one she offers.

Here the court must say plainly what neither side has been willing to concede, namely that capacity is not a single lamp that either burns or is out, but a thing that waxes and wanes with the hour and the subject; and the record contains a witness, the notary's clerk, able to speak to the particular morning rather than to the general condition.

The clerk, who was called to the house to read the holograph aloud before it was sealed, and whose memory the court finds neither rehearsed nor evasive, says that the testatrix corrected him twice on the spelling of the quarry's name, and that she asked, unprompted, whether a half-share could be left in parts — a question showing not only that she understood the asset but that she had been turning over its division, for a mind that invents difficulties for itself is not a mind being led, and the daughter, who sat in the kitchen throughout, did not prompt her.

That testimony obliges the court to prefer the holograph as the operative instrument, and the eldest son's challenge to the earlier will consequently loses its object.

But the matter does not end there; the holograph speaks only of the house and the accounts, leaves the quarry-share unmentioned, and so that portion must pass as on intestacy, since a testator's silence is not a disposition.

The son has an answer, and it is a good one: the eleven unpaid years were spent in the expectation of inheriting the terraces, and if the court permits the holograph to defeat that expectation while allowing no compensation, it will reward a promise made and honour only the paper that forgot it, leaving the labour unpriced and the house enriched at the labourer's cost.

The court accepts the premise and rejects the conclusion: the expectation was real, the terraces were worked, and the orchards the surveyor valued last spring owe their present worth to pruning no will recorded; yet an equitable charge, not a rewriting of the bequest, is the proper remedy, because a court that redrew testaments wherever it found unrequited effort would soon be writing more of them than the dead, and because the daughter's nursing was unpaid too, and cancelling one debt by inventing another would leave the estate poorer than the quarrel found it.

The order therefore stands as follows, and the parties will note that the figures depend on the valuation already filed.

The house and the bank accounts pass to the younger daughter under the holograph, subject to a charge of eleven thousand in favour of her brother, calculated at the rate the assessor applied to comparable orchard labour; the quarry-share, because the will is silent and the law is not, divides equally between them, unless they agree within sixty days upon a sale, in which case the proceeds follow the same division; and the costs of the capacity challenge fall upon the son, who pressed it after the clerk's deposition was disclosed to him. Judgment accordingly.

The estate of Ambrose Thelwall Pardoe, which consisted of a working orchard, a house of no architectural distinction, and a portfolio of municipal bonds, comes before this court in a condition of unusual clarity as to its contents and unusual murk as to its destination, for the testator wrote three wills in his last decade and destroyed only two of them; and the survivor, dated the eleventh of October, is challenged on two independent grounds, the first going to capacity, the second to a codicil said to have been executed under pressure; and the claimants, who are four in number and three in disposition, are content to argue in the alternative, each of them prepared to urge that the instrument stands if it benefits them, which the court notes without censure, and to urge that it falls if, when the devising words are read as the testator's own hand set them down, something must be found to carry the orchard elsewhere, since the orchard, as the inventory shows, is the only asset that anyone has troubled to weep over, carrying with it the water rights, and the water rights carry the neighbours' goodwill.

The eldest daughter, Honoria, who managed the orchard for nine seasons without wages, who has produced ledgers in her own careful hand, who asks the court to construe the residuary gift as a gift of the whole, advances a claim grounded in contribution rather than in text: she says she earned what the paper does not give her; because she planted, because she pruned, because she stayed when the others went to the coast and sent postcards.

Against her the second son, Rufus, sets a narrower and in some respects a stronger case: he does not dispute her labour, nor does he dispute that labour deserves recompense, though he insists that recompense is one thing and succession another.

Rufus relies upon the codicil of March, which names him as devisee of the orchard in terms admitting no ambiguity; and the handwriting expert, whose report I have read twice, finds no irregularity in the signature.

The difficulty lies elsewhere, in the circumstances attending that March afternoon, and two witnesses who were present give accounts that cannot both be true; the court is therefore obliged to weigh credibility, since no document can settle what documents are silent about; and here the third claimant intervenes, the nephew Crisp, who asks the court to disregard the codicil altogether.

Crisp, whose standing rests upon an earlier instrument that he has been careful to preserve, whose interest is adverse to both his cousins, argues that the testator's capacity had failed before March; and he points to the medical notes, which record confusion on three occasions, which record also a lucid interval in February, so that the picture is neither black nor white, and the court must decide whether the balance tips, bearing in mind that capacity is presumed until the contrary is shown, and the burden sits on the one who alleges incapacity.

That burden Crisp has not discharged: confusion about the day of the week does not establish inability to dispose of an orchard, and the notes record nothing worse.

I therefore uphold the codicil, so far as it goes; the orchard passes to Rufus; but the codicil does not touch the residue, and the residue includes the bonds, and the house falls to be divided under the surviving will, as that instrument directs.

There remains Honoria's claim in contribution, which stands outside the testamentary question altogether: she worked, and the estate was enriched; and because the enrichment is measurable, the ledgers being unchallenged, the court may award a charge upon the orchard, the charge being quantified at nine seasons' wages, and the valuation taken at the rate the testator paid his hired men.

The fourth claimant, Letitia, has filed nothing beyond a letter; her position is that she wants no part of it, and the court takes her at her word, though it records that her share is held for her against reconsideration; she may claim it within six years; the bonds will meanwhile be kept intact by the executor, who is directed to account annually, so that nothing is spent before she decides whether indifference is a settled policy or a passing temper.

The orchard, which has outlasted three wills and four tempers, will be in blossom by the time this order is drawn.

It is the court's view that such an outcome does less violence to the testator's intention than any alternative urged upon it, since the orchard goes to the son who was named, and the labour of the daughter is paid for out of the thing her labour preserved, while the absent child keeps a door open that she did not trouble to close; and the house, which nobody has asked for, is to be sold and the proceeds divided in equal fourths. Costs will be borne by the estate.

The estate of Verena Halloway, which was declared open on the third of November, presents a difficulty of a kind this court has rarely been asked to resolve, since the instrument offered for probate is undisputed in its execution and the capacity of the testatrix has not been impugned; yet the dispute persists, drawing its force from a single clause whose terms seem calculated to divide what they were intended to join, for the testatrix bequeathed the house at Fennel Lane to "my daughter who has remained," and three claimants have appeared, each insisting that remaining is a word the court must construe before anything else can follow, and each proposing a construction that would, if adopted, exclude the other two entirely.

The eldest, Ilse Halloway, who resided in the house for nineteen years, who paid the rates after her mother's second illness, who maintains that no other reading of the clause can be sustained without violence to the ordinary meaning of the English language, rests her claim on continuity of residence: she was in the house when the will was drawn, she was in the house when the codicil was refused, and she was in the house on the morning the estate fell open.

Against this the second claimant, Darrow Halloway, advances an argument of a different order: the testatrix, he says, never spoke of residence at all, since the phrase she chose carries a sense of fidelity rather than of address.

He relies upon four letters, which the court has examined and admitted, and upon the testimony of the parish solicitor: a man whose recollection, though imperfect in dates, is consistent in substance.

The third claimant, Ottilie Pye, who is not a daughter by blood but was adopted in 1981, asks the court to read the clause narrowly, since the testatrix knew precisely how to name her children when she wished to; and she offers a document, a household ledger, to show a pattern of designation.

What the court must decide, therefore, is whether a testamentary phrase capable of bearing three defensible senses is to be read against the surrounding instrument, which is silent, or against the external conduct of the parties, which is not; and here the authorities diverge, for one line of cases confines the inquiry to the four corners of the will, while another admits evidence of circumstance, provided the ambiguity is latent rather than patent, and the court is satisfied that the words themselves cannot be resolved by grammar alone.

This court takes the latter view, preferring to give effect to intention, and it regards the ambiguity here as plainly latent.

The clause is intelligible on its face; it names a daughter; it does not name which daughter, and it furnishes no criterion; it therefore invites extrinsic proof, unless the surrounding dispositions supply one.

They do not supply one. The residuary gift is general; the specific legacies are divided without reference to residence, and where the testatrix wished to distinguish between her children she did so by name, as the gift of the sideboard shows, as the gift of the annuity shows, and as the revoked codicil would have shown.

The court therefore turns to the evidence of conduct. The letters establish that the testatrix corresponded regularly with Darrow; they establish that she used the word "remained" of him twice, in a context that admits no reading but the figurative, since both letters were written while he was abroad. The ledger is of less assistance: it records payments to all three, which it enters under a common heading, so that nothing can be inferred from it as to preference, without assuming the very point in issue.

It follows that the first claimant's reading, which depends on an equation of remaining with residing, must fail.

The court accordingly declares that the house at Fennel Lane passes to Darrow Halloway, whose claim alone is consistent with the testatrix's own usage, and, since the second claimant takes the specific devise, the residue falls to be divided equally, as the instrument directs, under the clause that was never in contention; costs will follow the event, save that the third claimant, whose position was reasonably arguable, shall bear her own. The order is drawn accordingly.

The estate of Cornelia Whitlock, which passed under a will executed eleven months before her death, has come before this court in a condition of some disorder, for the testatrix signed two instruments in the same season and left neither formally revoked; and the second, though shorter, bears the more recent date. The dispute accordingly turns not upon the authenticity of either document but upon the intention that animated the later one, a question that cannot be settled by the paper alone, and the court must therefore ask whether the second instrument was drawn to supplement the first or to displace it, a difficulty sharpened by the fact that the two are not in every respect inconsistent, since property disposed of in the earlier will is simply unmentioned in the later, so that to read the second as a total revocation would require the court to assume, where the testatrix said nothing, that silence was meant to operate as a positive erasure, thereby cancelling gifts she had taken pains to describe and leaving a portion of her estate to fall into intestacy.

The elder son, Dominic, who takes the whole residue under the second instrument, who was present when it was signed, who urges that its very brevity was deliberate, asks the court to treat the later paper as a complete and self-sufficient disposition; his argument is one of simplicity. A later will speaks last. Brevity is not ambiguity. The testatrix knew what she was leaving out.

The force of this submission is not small, since a testator is presumed to understand the instrument she executes, and the law does not ordinarily rescue the disappointed from the consequences of a relative's plain words.

But simplicity is a virtue of argument, not a rule of construction, and the presumption Dominic invokes is itself conditional; it operates only where the words are plain.

Here they are not. The second instrument, which the solicitor's attendance note describes as having been prepared in haste during an illness, contains no revocation clause at all; and the omission is not a drafting flourish, it is the absence of the one sentence that would have made Dominic's reading unanswerable.

The daughter, Marguerite, who takes the farmland under the first will, whose interest the second instrument never mentions, presses the opposite construction, and she does so from the same premise her brother relies upon, namely that the testatrix was a careful woman who had used a revocation clause in the earlier document and who would not have abandoned the formula without purpose, so that the only purpose the court can plausibly attribute to her is an intention to leave the earlier dispositions standing wherever the later paper did not touch them, since a careful testatrix does not revoke by accident, and the burden of showing revocation lies with the party asserting it.

I find this reasoning sound, though it does not carry Marguerite as far as she would like, and it leaves the residue untouched.

The younger son, Peter, seeks to go further, claiming that the second instrument is void altogether; his case rests on capacity, and he points to the solicitor's note, which records confusion, and he urges that the brevity Dominic praises is itself the symptom of a failing mind, though the evidence is thin.

An attendance note is not a medical opinion. The solicitor recorded confusion about dates, not about property, and the witnesses spoke of a woman who was tired but lucid, who recognised her children, who named her farm, who asked twice whether the paper was ready.

Capacity, in this court, is measured against the task undertaken, and the task undertaken that afternoon was a short one; the testatrix was asked to say who should have what remained after the specific gifts, and she answered that question without hesitation, in terms that the witnesses, who had no interest in the outcome, repeated to me without variation. Peter's challenge therefore fails. The second instrument stands as a partial disposition, which it was drafted to be, and I construe the two wills together as a single testamentary scheme, so that the farmland passes to Marguerite under the earlier instrument, where the gift was expressed with a particularity the later paper nowhere disturbs, while the residue, including the proceeds of the London lease, passes to Dominic under the second, and the costs of all parties will come out of the estate, since the confusion was the testatrix's own making. Let the order be drawn accordingly.

The estate of Ardith Venable, which consisted of a quarry no longer worked, a house above it, and a bank account of unremarkable size, passes now to this court for division, because the testatrix left two instruments and the later one was never properly witnessed; the first names her nephew Corin sole legatee, and the second, drawn eleven months afterward, divides the whole among three grandnieces, and so the court must decide whether the defective paper may yet speak, for a document that fails in its execution may still establish, if the circumstances allow the inference to stand, that the maker had resolved to revoke what she had earlier set down, so that the earlier gift, though formally intact, would be hollow, leaving the estate to pass as if no will had been made at all.

Corin Venable, who worked the quarry for nine seasons without wages, who nursed his aunt through the last winter of her illness, who argues that her intention never altered toward him, contends that the second instrument was extracted rather than composed; and his argument has weight, since the testatrix was by then nearly blind, since the paper is in the hand of the eldest grandniece, since no disinterested person stood in the room when the signature was affixed.

The grandnieces answer with a different account of that room: the paper was read aloud twice, slowly, by a neighbor who has since died, though the neighbor's presence rests on a single remembered remark.

Their counsel presses a further point, which the court cannot dismiss without reasons: an aunt who knows herself dying commonly reaches past the nearest claimant, and the record shows letters, sixteen of them, in which the testatrix speaks of the girls with evident warmth.

Yet warmth is not the measure the law applies, and the statute, which demands two witnesses and admits no equivalent, does not inquire whether the maker felt generous; the court is not free to supply what the legislature withheld, however the equities may lean; and so the second instrument fails as a will, a conclusion that does not end the matter but obliges the court to look again at the first.

The question that now opens, which Corin's counsel prefers to leave shut, is whether the failed instrument, void as a disposition, may nevertheless operate as evidence of revocation; and here the authorities divide, for some hold that an unexecuted paper is a nullity for every purpose, while others, which this court finds more persuasive, admit it where the revoking intent is manifest from the text itself, and admit it further where the surrounding conduct confirms that intent, allowing the earlier gift to lapse once the maker has plainly turned from it, and the record leaves no doubt that she had.

The deciding fact is the condition of the first will: the testatrix kept it, to be sure, but she had drawn her pen through the clause naming her nephew.

That mark must be given effect, to cancel what it crosses; the paper is not ambiguous; the ink matches the second instrument and the stroke runs the full width of the line, and no one has suggested that another hand made it, though the nephew has had every occasion to do so.

The court therefore holds the first will revoked as to the legacy: the estate falls into intestacy, and the statutory scheme governs the distribution, which divides the property among the four surviving relations in equal shares, so that the nephew takes a quarter and each grandniece takes a quarter likewise.

This result will satisfy nobody entirely, and the court does not pretend otherwise: the nephew receives less than his labor earned, and the grandnieces receive less than their aunt's last paper promised them, a paper that failed for want of two signatures and nothing graver; still, there is a justice in the outcome that the parties may come to see, which lies in this, that the law refuses to guess at the dead while it will not shut its eyes to what the dead have plainly done, cancelling where she cancelled but declining to give where she did not give in the form required.

The quarry, which cannot be divided in kind, shall be sold and the proceeds apportioned.

Costs are to be borne by the estate, which is the only fund that bears them fairly, since neither side brought this action in bad faith and neither side could have resolved it privately, as the defect in the paper was one that no agreement among the parties could have cured; and the court records its regret that a woman so careful in her affections was so careless with a pen, though carelessness of that kind is the commonest matter on this docket. Judgment accordingly.
